questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a suspensive veto from a veto of annulment

options.text: It permanently cancels the law, so that the vetoing body need not vote again on it.
options.misconception: conflates suspension with annulment

options.text: It has no effect until the law has entered into force and begun to cause harm.
options.misconception: limits the veto to a moment of transition

options.text: It suspends the law's operation until the vetoing body votes again, and the law stands if the veto is not sustained.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare a technocratic government with an ordinary caretaker cabinet
questions.stem: Group handout item 4: the group asks what distinguishes a technocratic government from an ordinary caretaker cabinet; explain the differences.

answer.exemplar: A technocratic government is distinguished by the source and quality of its authority rather than by its temporary character alone. Its members are selected for technical expertise rather than party standing, it normally enjoys only a narrow or shifting parliamentary majority, and it is expected to govern for a limited period and for a defined purpose such as a budget or an institutional reform. Because it lacks an ordinary partisan base, it cannot rely on the machinery of party discipline to carry measures through the legislature and must seek agreement across the chamber or use devices such as ordinances. A caretaker cabinet shares the temporariness but retains party political responsibility and exists only to manage routine business until an election, whereas a technocratic cabinet claims to act on the country rather than on a party.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of a technocratic government and a caretaker cabinet. A strong answer distinguishes expertise-based authority from temporariness and notes the parliamentary cost.
questions.hint: Compare the source of authority, not just the duration.

stimulus.body: The standing orders provide that a suspensive veto may be overridden by an absolute majority of the members of the assembly, counted on the day of the vote, and that members who abstain are recorded as present but their votes are not counted towards either side. questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the fixed-term guarantee and its limits

stimulus.body: A working paper describes the fixed term of the legislature as a guarantee supplied by the rules on dissolution. Because the executive cannot dissolve the legislature at will, the assembly's term runs to its appointed end regardless of the government's fortunes, and a government that loses its majority must either continue governing as a minority or seek a new election through the mechanism the rules provide. The paper adds that the guarantee is not absolute, because the rules usually allow a dissolution on certain conditions, such as the failure of a confidence vote.

questions.stem: Discussion log item 7: on the strength of the extract, which option best describes the fixed-term guarantee?

options.text: It guarantees that the legislature serves the full term whatever happens, since dissolution is never permitted.
options.misconception: ignores the dissolution routes the extract describes

options.text: It guarantees the legislature's independence from the executive, subject to defined dissolution routes.
It guarantees that the government must remain in office for the whole legislative term.
options.misconception: confuses the legislature's term with the government's tenure

options.text: It guarantees that the executive may dissolve the legislature whenever the government loses confidence.
options.misconception: makes dissolution a routine executive privilege

questions.explanation: The fixed-term guarantee protects the legislature's tenure against executive dissolution, subject to defined routes. Absolute immunity, government tenure and routine dissolution each misread the extract.
questions.hint: Ask what the guarantee protects and what it excludes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the problem a lapse-of-time rule for signature solves
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 8: the group asks why a lapse-of-time rule for signature was introduced and what it achieves; explain the problem it solves.

answer.exemplar: The problem the rule solves is the accumulation of texts that the executive has adopted but has not signed. Where signature is needed to make a decision operative, and no time limit applies, a government can adopt a great many texts, leave them unsigned, and so hold a volume of unexecuted or uncertain law that it may either sign later or quietly drop, at the election or after a change of government. A lapse-of-time rule converts that open-ended situation into a closed one: once the statutory period passes without signature, the text is deemed never to have been adopted and disappears from the government's programme without any further act. The cost is that a government must now actively sign what it wants, and cannot keep options open by the simple device of silence.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of the problem a lapse-of-time rule solves. A strong answer identifies the accumulation of unsigned texts and the closure it imposes on executive choices.
questions.hint: Think about what unexecuted and unsigned texts accumulate.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Junior minister and minister of state
questions.learningObjective: Compare the ranks of junior minister and minister of state
questions.stem: Practice sheet item 12: the group asks how a minister of state differs from a junior minister in a French-style government; explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: The distinction is one of rank and of the range of business handled, not a difference between politicians and technicians. A junior minister, holding the more junior title, is normally attached to a particular portfolio and to a senior minister who holds the overall responsibility for that area, and it is the senior minister who signs the acts in that field and answers for them. A minister of state sits at the senior end of the governmental hierarchy, above junior ministers and below the head of government, and carries a portfolio or a coordination brief of its own that may cross departmental lines. The practical consequence is that responsibility for a field is divided between an official who decides and one who holds the political title, and disputes about who is accountable for a failure often turn on which of the two the relevant act was signed by.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of the two ministerial ranks. A strong answer explains the hierarchy, the division of portfolio responsibility and who signs the acts.
questions.hint: Ask which office holds the portfolio and which signs.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two different override thresholds

stimulus.body: The committee note describes three thresholds that appear in the review of veto override rules. Where a suspensive veto may be overridden by an absolute majority of the assembly, the threshold is expressed as more than half of all members, and abstentions are not counted for either side. Where the assembly may override by a two-thirds vote, the threshold is expressed in terms of two thirds of the members present and voting, and abstentions are excluded from the calculation entirely. The note observes that the two expressions are frequently confused in summaries of the rules.

questions.stem: Seminar notes item 14: on the strength of the extract, which option best states the distinction the note draws?

It distinguishes a veto overridable by the executive alone from one overridable only by the legislature.
options.misconception: invents an executive override the note does not describe

options.text: It shows that the two expressions are interchangeable, since both require a supermajority.
options.misconception: collapses two different thresholds into one

questions.explanation: The note separates a threshold of more than half of all members from a two-thirds threshold of members present and voting. Reversing the two, an executive override and interchangeability each misread it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare systems with and without a fixed legislative term

stimulus.body: A study compares two ways of securing the continuity of the legislature. Under the first, the assembly serves a fixed term and the executive may not dissolve it except on defined conditions, so that the government cannot arrange a fresh election whenever its position becomes uncomfortable. Under the second, the government is allowed to dissolve the legislature freely, and the guarantee against arbitrary dissolution is replaced by the legislature's own power to remove the government by a vote of no confidence.

questions.stem: Study memo item 15: on the strength of the extract, which option best captures the difference between the two systems?

options.text: The first gives the government more control over the electoral calendar than the second.
options.misconception: reverses which system restricts the executive

options.text: The second guarantees the legislature a fixed term, because dissolution leaves the assembly intact.
options.misconception: treats dissolution as harmless to the assembly

options.text: The two are equivalent, since a no-confidence vote always produces the same result as a dissolution.
options.misconception: asserts the two mechanisms are interchangeable

options.text: The first protects the legislature's term, while the second protects the government against a hostile assembly.

questions.explanation: The fixed term protects the legislature by limiting dissolution, while free dissolution shifts protection to the government. Reversed control, equivalence and harmless dissolution each misread the comparison.
questions.hint: Ask which office each system protects.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a signature time limit affects an election-facing government
questions.stem: Group handout item 16: the group asks how a lapse-of-time rule for signature interacts with a government that wants to keep options open before an election; explain the interaction.

answer.exemplar: A government preparing for an election has an obvious reason to keep unsettled questions unsettled, and a lapse-of-time rule narrows but does not remove that freedom. Before the rule, texts could be adopted and left unsigned indefinitely, so the government could hold a stock of measures ready for use once a future parliament had returned, or could abandon them without admitting defeat. Once a time limit applies, the stock must be worked through: a text that is not signed within the period lapses and must be re-adopted, re-submitted and re-signed if it is still wanted. The government therefore faces a choice between signing measures it may not want to enact and letting them die, and it must make that choice on a timetable set by the rule rather than by the electoral calendar. The pressure this creates is precisely the point of the device.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how the signature rule affects an election-facing government. A strong answer explains the closing of options and the timetable it imposes.
questions.hint: Think about the choice between signing and letting texts lapse.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a technocratic government leans on ordinances
questions.stem: Group handout item 20: the group asks why a technocratic government often has to rely on measures issued by ordinance; explain the reason.

answer.exemplar: A technocratic government is appointed for expertise and lacks the ordinary partisan machinery that carries a programme through a legislature. Its majority, if it has one, is a negotiated or shifting arrangement that cannot be relied on to hold for the length of a budget or an institutional reform, and the parties that appointed the cabinet may themselves be fragmented. Under those conditions, passing an ordinary law becomes uncertain, and the instrument of the ordinance, which allows the executive to legislate subject to later ratification, becomes the route of least resistance. The trade is familiar: speed and certainty in exchange for a weaker connection between the measure and the legislature's own deliberations, and a risk that ratification will fail or be delayed, which can in turn require the government to fall back on even more limited powers.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written explanation of why a technocratic government leans on ordinances. A strong answer links the absent reliable majority to the instrument's speed and its dependence on ratification.
questions.hint: Think about what the government cannot count on in the chamber.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difficulty a signature time limit creates on resignation
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 24: the group asks how a lapse-of-time rule interacts with ministerial resignations; explain the difficulty that creates.

answer.exemplar: A lapse-of-time rule and a ministerial resignation pull in opposite directions, because the rule assumes that a responsible minister will be available to sign within the period allowed. If a minister resigns, the texts he was to sign cannot be signed by him, and the government must either appoint a successor who will assume responsibility for them or risk the texts lapsing under the rule. The difficulty is that the succession is itself a political act: a successor may refuse to adopt the policy of the outgoing minister, in which case the texts must be re-examined rather than merely re-signed, and if no successor is appointed in time the lapse operates on the government's own initiative rather than on a deliberate decision to abandon the measure. A well-drafted rule therefore provides that the period begins to run only when the office is filled, so that a vacancy does not silently dispose of measures the government still wants.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of the interaction between a signature time limit and ministerial resignations. A strong answer explains the risk of silent lapse and the response of delaying the clock.
questions.hint: Think about who signs when the office is vacant.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why override arithmetic is harder than passage arithmetic
questions.stem: Group handout item 28: the group asks why override arithmetic is often harder than the arithmetic of passing a law; explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: Passing a law and overriding a veto are arithmetically similar but politically different, and the difference is what makes the second harder. The vote to override usually requires a higher figure or a different base than the vote to pass, because the veto exists precisely to make the second stage more demanding, and it is typically the chamber with the weaker political position that holds the veto. The arithmetic also tends to be less visible, since a government that can assemble a majority to pass a measure may not know whether the same combination is present for an override on a different day, and the numbers must be recomputed each time. Members who abstained or voted with the government on the first reading may not do so again, and the discipline of the governing parties may be harder to enforce when the vote is presented as a test of the government rather than of a measure. That is why override arithmetic is the part of the rules that governments most often misjudge.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of passing a law and overriding a veto. A strong answer identifies the differently based threshold and the difficulty of recomputing support.
questions.hint: Think about which vote needs the bigger number.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a suspensive veto alters the legislative calendar
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 32: the group asks how a suspensive veto changes the timing of the legislative process; explain the consequences for the calendar of a law.

answer.exemplar: A suspensive veto inserts a second stage into the making of a law, and every consequence for the timetable follows from that insertion. Where the first vote is in the chamber that originated the law, the second vote takes place in the vetoing chamber, so the law must be transmitted, calendared there, and voted on a second time, which commonly adds weeks or months to the process. During that interval the law's entry into force is suspended, so the executive must plan around a gap between adoption and operation and may be tempted to fill the gap with other instruments. The second vote is also a fresh occasion on which the arithmetic changes, because the composition of the second chamber differs from that of the first and because the parties may reposition between the readings. A government with a working majority in both chambers is therefore largely indifferent to the procedure, while a government that expects to lose the second vote may seek to amend the law in the interval, and a law that must serve the whole term is drafted with the second reading in view from the start.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks how a suspensive veto alters the legislative calendar. A strong answer traces the added stage, the suspended entry into force and the bargaining between readings.
questions.hint: Think about the extra stage the law must pass through.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the end of a term accelerates decisions
questions.stem: Group handout item 36: the group asks how the end of the legislative term can be used to accelerate decisions that would otherwise stall; explain the mechanism.

answer.exemplar: The mechanism is the altered bargaining position created by the approaching election, reinforced in some systems by rules that let the government take certain decisions by a lighter procedure when the legislature's term is about to expire. Administratively, a fixed calendar applies: measures must be tabled before a cut-off date if they are to be debated at all, so that the chamber can complete its business before dissolution, and the government's own programme has to be prepared against that date rather than against an open timetable. Politically, the party or parties that expect to win have every reason to see measures they favour adopted before the electorate replaces them, while the outgoing majority may calculate that obstructing them costs more in the campaign than accepting them. The result is a burst of activity near the end of the term in which decisions that seemed impossible in the middle of the term are taken quickly, because the costs of delay have become concentrated and visible.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks how the end of a term accelerates decisions. A strong answer combines the fixed cut-off calendar with the changed electoral incentives for the outgoing majority.
questions.hint: Think about deadlines and what an election changes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare design options for the suspensive veto
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 40: the group asks how a suspensive veto could be made to work better in practice; explain the design options.

answer.exemplar: The design options all bear on the interval between the two votes, because that is where the suspensive veto does its work. A time limit can be attached to the second vote, so that a veto must be confirmed or the law proceeds, which removes the possibility of indefinitely suspending legislation. The first reading can be strengthened by requiring a wider majority in the vetoing chamber for the veto itself to be entertained, which raises the cost of using it frivolously while leaving its protective value intact. The scope of the veto can be limited to the provisions objected to, so that a disputed schedule does not hold up the whole measure. Alternatively, a fast-track procedure can be created for the bills the executive most needs, exempting them from the veto altogether, which trades a wider exception for the protection of ordinary legislation. Each option shifts the balance slightly, and each shifts it against someone: the chamber that holds the veto loses some of its reach, while the chamber that passes the bills gains a little speed.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of design options for the suspensive veto. A strong answer works through time limits, filtered vetoes, qualified majorities and exemptions, and who bears the cost.
questions.hint: Consider the interval between the two votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a technocratic cabinet typically falls
questions.stem: Group handout item 44: the group asks how the fall of a technocratic cabinet is likely to work; explain the usual sequence.

answer.exemplar: A technocratic cabinet usually falls without any of the drama attached to a partisan defeat. It was never entitled to assume the confidence of the chamber, so it is built on negotiated understandings that can be withdrawn one at a time, and the resignation of a single minister may be enough to show that the understandings no longer hold. The head of government may then offer his resignation before a vote, on the argument that the programme can no longer be carried and that the legislature should be given the opportunity to try someone else. If the legislature declines to engage with the programme, a vote of no confidence may follow, but the government may already have gone, and in either case the succession is settled by an agreement among the parties rather than by a contest. The distinctive feature is the absence of a political alternative waiting to take over: the parties that appointed the cabinet may have no agreed successor, which is why cabinets of this kind are sometimes described as governing until the last possible moment.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how a technocratic cabinet typically falls. A strong answer notes the negotiated understandings, the offered resignation and the absence of a successor.
questions.hint: Think about how the cabinet's support was assembled.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fixed term reshapes the government-opposition relationship
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 48: the group asks how a fixed-term guarantee affects the relationship between government and opposition across the term; explain the consequences.

answer.exemplar: A fixed term removes the government's ability to choose the moment of its own defeat, and that changes the relationship with the opposition in two directions. For the opposition, the guarantee is a guarantee of time: it can prepare its alternative programme and its own candidates without fear that the calendar will be reset against it by a dissolution, and it can compel the government to face the chamber for the whole period. For the government, the guarantee is a discipline, because a defeat in the chamber cannot be turned into a new election at a moment of its choosing, and ministers must therefore either find a way to govern with a minority or negotiate with the parties that hold the balance. What the guarantee does not do is remove the possibility of an early election, since the rules typically allow a dissolution on defined conditions; the effect is that the exception must be argued for rather than assumed, which changes who bears the burden of justification in every period of the term.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of how a fixed term reshapes the government-opposition relationship. A strong answer covers the opposition's time and the discipline imposed on the government.

questions.learningObjective: Compute the share of texts that would lapse unsigned
questions.stem: Seminar notes item 50: the government adopted 40 texts in a session and signed 31; what percentage of the adopted texts would lapse if the rule gives ministers 20 days to sign and the rest were never signed?

options.text: The adopted texts that would lapse are 77.5 per cent, since 31 of the 40 were signed.
options.misconception: reports the signed share as the lapsing share

options.text: The adopted texts that would lapse are 22.5 per cent, since 9 of the 40 were left unsigned.
The adopted texts that would lapse are 9 per cent, since 9 of the 100 possible texts were unsigned.
options.misconception: uses an invented denominator of one hundred texts

options.text: No text would lapse, because the rule applies only to texts submitted after the session.
options.misconception: invents a scope limit the rule does not contain

questions.explanation: Nine of the 40 adopted texts were left unsigned, and 9 divided by 40 is 22.5 per cent, so that share would be deemed never adopted. The share signed or the absolute count misleads.
questions.hint: Count the unsigned texts and divide by the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Junior minister and minister of state
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a minister of state exercises authority without a portfolio
questions.stem: Study memo item 51: the group asks how a minister of state who holds no separate portfolio can still exercise authority; explain how that works.

options.text: He coordinates across portfolios and may be given specific files, exercising authority in the name of the government.
He inherits the powers of the head of government whenever that office is vacant.
options.misconception: invents a succession rule for the head of government

options.text: He holds a purely ceremonial rank with no function beyond attending cabinet meetings.
options.misconception: denies the coordinating role the title carries

options.text: He may veto the acts of any junior minister attached to a different minister.
options.misconception: invents a veto power that the rank does not carry

questions.explanation: A minister of state without a portfolio of his own coordinates across departmental boundaries and may be entrusted with particular files. Succession to the head of government, a purely ceremonial role and a veto over other ministers each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask what a minister of state does across departments.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the closing months can free a government to act
questions.stem: Group handout item 52: the group asks why the final months of a term are sometimes described as the only period in which a government can act freely; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The freedom is relative rather than absolute, but the comparison with the middle of the term is instructive. A government that still faces an election has every reason to postpone measures that will divide its own majority, to preserve the appearance of unity for the campaign, and to avoid handing the opposition a rallying point; the resulting caution is not a legal restraint but a political one, and it operates most strongly on the measures that would cost the government most in the vote. Near the end of the term that calculation changes. The government no longer needs to win anything, the campaign will not be influenced by measures it adopts, and the opposition's incentive to object may itself fall away as members concentrate on their own constituencies. What the government gains is therefore not freedom from constraint but freedom from the particular constraint of the election, and the corollary is that a government that has used the middle of the term to prepare, and has the parliamentary numbers to carry measures, can complete more in the last weeks than in the whole year before.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written account of why the closing months can free a government to act. A strong answer contrasts electoral caution with the absence of electoral stakes at the end.
questions.hint: Think about what the government still stands to win.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute an override threshold net of vacant seats
questions.stem: Revision card item 53: a chamber of 150 seats has 10 vacancies, and the rule requires more than half of the members entitled to vote to override a suspensive veto; how many votes are needed?
questions.explanation: With 10 of the 150 seats vacant, 140 members may vote, and more than half of 140 means at least 71 votes. Measuring against the full 150 or treating half as enough misreads the threshold.
questions.hint: Exclude the vacancies before halving the entitlement.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Describe the possible outcomes for an emergency ordinance

stimulus.body: The handbook explains the lifecycle of an emergency ordinance. The government signs the ordinance, which then operates without prior legislative approval, and submits the text to the legislature. The legislature may ratify it, in which case the measure becomes an ordinary law; it may amend it, in which case the amended text becomes the law; or it may take no decision, in which case the ordinance lapses at the end of the period allowed for ratification. The handbook notes that the lapse is automatic and does not require any further act of the legislature or of the government.

questions.stem: Workshop sheet item 54: on the strength of the extract, which option best captures the possible outcomes of the ordinance?

options.text: Ratification, amendment or lapse by the passage of time if the legislature does not decide in time.
Ratification or repeal only, since the legislature must either adopt or reject the text as it stands.
options.misconception: omits the amending possibility the handbook records

options.text: Continuation in force until the legislature acts, however long that takes.
options.misconception: denies the automatic lapse of the text

options.text: Immediate annulment by the government, which may withdraw the text before ratification is complete.
options.misconception: invents a withdrawal power the handbook does not describe

questions.explanation: The handbook records three routes: ratification, amendment of the text, and automatic lapse when the legislature takes no decision within the period allowed. A binary choice, indefinite continuation and a withdrawal power each misread the lifecycle.
questions.hint: Ask what happens if the legislature neither adopts nor amends.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the fragility of a technocratic cabinet's claim to neutrality

stimulus.body: An assessment notes that a technocratic cabinet is often described as neutral, and that the description is doing more work than it appears. It explains that the cabinet is chosen without regard to party, that its programme is presented as a technical necessity rather than a political preference, and that its members expect to leave office once the programme is done. The assessment warns that the claim of neutrality cannot survive a contested political decision, because the moment the cabinet must choose between competing claims it is making a political choice like any other government, and the parties will begin to treat it as partisan.

questions.stem: Discussion log item 55: on the strength of the extract, which option best captures the assessment's point?

options.text: The claim of neutrality is well founded, since technocratic cabinets are chosen without regard to party.
options.misconception: accepts the claim of neutrality at face value

options.text: The claim of neutrality is fragile, since a contested political choice exposes the cabinet as partisan.
The cabinet is expected to remain in office after the programme ends, so its neutrality is not tested.
options.misconception: inverts the assessment on the cabinet's expected tenure

options.text: The parties have no reason to treat a technocratic cabinet as partisan, because it decides on technical grounds.
options.misconception: denies the political reading of technical decisions

questions.explanation: The assessment shows that the neutrality of a technocratic cabinet is a claim that political choices will erode, since the cabinet must eventually choose between competing claims. Accepted neutrality, an untested tenure and a purely technical reading each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when a technical choice becomes contested.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare design options for a fixed-term guarantee
questions.stem: Syllabus page item 56: the group asks how the fixed-term guarantee could be designed to serve stability better; explain the design options.

answer.exemplar: The design options all address the same weakness, which is that a fixed term can become a fixed term in which no majority exists for the whole of its duration. The most common remedy is a provision for dissolution on a defined condition, such as the failure of a confidence motion, which lets the electorate arbitrate when the chamber and the government are in genuine deadlock; the cost is that the condition may be satisfied for tactical reasons, so the rule is usually drafted to require a qualified vote and to bind the executive to ask the question rather than to decide it. A second option is a constructive vote of no confidence, which makes the opposition nominate an alternative before the government can be removed, so that the assembly is never left without a candidate government. A third is a mid-term review mechanism, under which the government's programme is confirmed at a fixed point, which does not dissolve anything but forces the government to demonstrate support. A fourth is simply to shorten the term, which reduces the period in which a government can be sustained without a majority at the cost of more frequent elections.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks for a written comparison of design options for the fixed-term guarantee. A strong answer covers conditional dissolution, constructive no confidence, mid-term review and shorter terms.
questions.hint: Think about how a government without a majority is handled.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of absences on an absolute-majority threshold
questions.stem: Revision sheet item 57: the group asks what happens to the arithmetic of an override when a quarter of the members are absent; explain the effect where an absolute majority of the whole chamber is required.

options.text: The threshold falls with the absentees, so a smaller number of votes suffices.
options.misconception: reduces the threshold when members are absent

options.text: The threshold is unchanged, since the whole chamber is still the basis of the calculation.
No override is possible while a quarter of the members are absent.
options.misconception: treats absence as an absolute bar on overriding

options.text: The threshold rises, because the absentees count against the override automatically.
options.misconception: counts absent members against the override

questions.explanation: Where the threshold is expressed as a majority of the whole chamber, absentees neither help nor hinder: the requirement is simply more than half of all members. A falling threshold, an absolute bar and a rising threshold each misdescribe the arithmetic.
questions.hint: Ask whether the threshold is a share of the chamber or of those voting.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a pattern of enactments across two periods
questions.stem: Seminar notes item 58: a chamber's log shows 12 bills enacted in the final three months of a term and 34 in the six months before that; what does the pattern suggest?

options.text: Enactment is concentrated near the end of the term, which is consistent with a burst of activity after a slower middle.
The chamber was idle for most of the term and rushed to clear a backlog before dissolution.
options.misconception: infers a backlog the figures do not establish

options.text: Bills are counted by the date of their tabling, so the totals say nothing about the passage of laws.
options.misconception: assumes a counting convention the log does not state

options.text: The figures show that the final three months saw 12 times as much legislation as the preceding six.
options.misconception: misreads the ratio between the two periods

questions.explanation: Thirty-four bills in six months followed by 12 in three months is a burst of activity at the end of the term, which fits a government with no further election to win. A cleared backlog, an irrelevant counting rule and a twelvefold ratio each misread the figures.
questions.hint: Compare the rate per month in each period.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Junior minister and minister of state
questions.learningObjective: Explain why junior ministers strengthen a government's capacity to act
questions.stem: Study memo item 59: the group asks why the presence of junior ministers is often said to strengthen a government's capacity to act; explain the reasoning.

options.text: Because junior ministers provide the votes that the government's own majority lacks.
options.misconception: confuses ministerial staffing with parliamentary numbers

options.text: Because senior ministers can delegate detailed work, which frees them for direction and oversight.
Because a larger cabinet makes the government harder to challenge in the legislature.
options.misconception: mistakes a larger bench for a stronger one

options.text: Because junior ministers are appointed on merit, so the cabinet's decisions improve.
options.misconception: reduces the benefit to a claim about appointment

questions.explanation: Junior ministers allow senior ministers to delegate detailed work and concentrate on direction, which is the capacity gain the arrangement produces. Parliamentary votes, an unchallengeable bench and appointment quality each misdescribe it.
questions.hint: Ask what senior ministers are freed to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the length of the signature period matters
questions.stem: Group handout item 60: the group asks why the choice of period in a lapse-of-time rule matters; explain the considerations involved.

answer.exemplar: The length of the period determines how much of the government's programme can still be left open, so it is a question about the balance between flexibility and certainty rather than a technical detail. A long period allows a government to sign texts at its convenience, to accommodate ministers who need time to consider them, and to keep options alive across a political transition, but it also leaves a substantial stock of adopted but unexecuted law, whose status is unclear and which a successor government may treat as valid. A short period forces the government to decide quickly, which suits a programme with a clear timetable and a disciplined cabinet, but it penalises measures that require consultation, and it may cause texts to lapse for reasons of scheduling rather than of policy. The drafting therefore has to match the character of the executive: a period long enough to allow signature after genuine consideration, but short enough that nothing remains indefinitely in the drawer, and often accompanied by a rule that the period begins only when the responsible office is filled.

questions.explanation: The prompt asks what depends on the length of the signature period. A strong answer sets flexibility against certainty and notes the effects on ministers, transitions and successors.
questions.hint: Think about what a long and a short period each allow.
